paragraphes: At school, you have to follow a set of rules. No phones in class, be on time, hand in your homework.
But that is not the only list of rules. Your sports club has its own. So does your family.
To know what is expected of you, you must learn all these rules, then follow them. For a company, this is called compliance.

decouverte.comme: Every place has its rules: school, the club, home. Being in line means knowing which ones apply to you and following them.
decouverte.enVrai: A company must follow several kinds of rules: laws, regulations, standards from its industry, and contracts. Compliance means doing what is needed to understand all of them and satisfy all of them. The picture stops there: at school, someone reminds you of the rules. In a company, it is up to the company to find out which rules apply.

decouverte.question: A company follows every security rule that applies to it. Is it automatically well protected?
options: Yes, following the rules is enough
No, it is a good base but only a first step
Only if an inspector has checked it
decouverte.answer: No, it is a good base but only a first step
decouverte.explanation: The official manual says compliance is a solid base, but only the first step. Following the rules does not mean being safe. The other two answers are tempting.

decouverte.texte: An online shop sells clothes. It follows the law on its customers' data, like their names and addresses. It respects the rules for card payments. It also keeps the promises in its contracts with suppliers. Three kinds of rules, one shop.

decouverte.comme: Getting the pass mark is the minimum to move up a year. It does not mean you have mastered the whole course.
decouverte.enVrai: Being compliant means reaching the minimum that is asked. Being truly protected often takes more. Compliance is a starting point, not the finish line.

cards.question: Official definition: “compliance”
cards.answer: (ISC)2 defines compliance as adherence to a mandate; it includes the set of activities that an organization conducts to understand and satisfy all applicable laws, regulatory requirements, industry standards, and contractual agreements.
cards.explanation: Think of the school rules: learn them, then really follow them.
cards.explanation_more: Definition from the official (ISC)2 manual, domain 1, section “Determine Compliance and Other Requirements”. (ISC)2 is the organization that awards the CISSP certificate. Learn it word for word: the next cards help you step by step.

cards.explanation: Two ideas: following an obligation (adherence), and satisfying every kind of rule, even the ones in contracts.

cards.explanation: Three blocks: following an obligation, understanding then satisfying the rules, and industry standards.

cards.question: A company has ticked every box in its rulebooks. What does the manual say about its security?
cards.answer: It has a solid base, but this is only a start
cards.explanation: Compliance is a good starting point. Security means going further.

cards.question: Where do compliance expectations come from?
cards.answer: From laws and regulations that apply to every industry. Others are specific to certain industries or products.
cards.explanation: Some rules are for everyone, others only for your field.
cards.explanation_more: Source: (ISC)2 manual, domain 1, section “Legislative and Regulatory Requirements”.

cards.question: Who imposes each obligation?
cards.answer: The government: the passed law, the agency rule and the data law. Contract or industry: the payment contract, the card brands rule and the agreement with the client.
cards.explanation: A law or a regulation comes from a public authority. A contract or an industry standard comes from an agreement between companies.

A rule written by a public agency
A law on protecting customers' data
The contract signed with the service that handles payments
A rule set by the big bank card brands
A security agreement signed with a big customer

cards.question: Why must a company review its compliance regularly?
cards.answer: Because expectations keep changing. It must check all the time that information is protected under every rule in force.
cards.explanation: What was in line yesterday may not be tomorrow.
cards.explanation_more: Source: (ISC)2 manual, domain 1, section “Legislative and Regulatory Requirements”: a set of constantly changing expectations that needs continuous review.

cards.question: Being compliant is only the [[first]] step toward [[security]].
cards.answer: Being compliant is only the first step toward security.
cards.explanation: You follow the rules, then you go further.

cards.question: Someone tells you: “Our company is compliant.” What do you really know?
cards.answer: That it follows the rules that apply to it
cards.explanation: Compliant means in line with the rules. It does not guarantee that no weakness exists.
options: That it follows the rules that apply to it

cards.question: In the definition, what does “adherence to a mandate” mean?
cards.answer: Following an obligation (a mandate): not only knowing it, but really sticking to it.
cards.explanation: Adherence means sticking to the rule and following it.

cards.question: A colleague says: “We are compliant, so we are safe.” What do you answer?
cards.answer: Compliance is a solid base, but only the first step. You can follow every rule and still have weaknesses. You must go further.
cards.explanation: Think of the pass mark: it lets you move up, but it does not prove you have mastered everything.

cards.question: What if a company ignores a rule that applies to it?
cards.answer: It is no longer compliant: it no longer satisfies all the rules that apply. The definition says to understand and then satisfy every one of them.
cards.explanation: One forgotten rule is enough to fall out of compliance.

cards.question: Why must a CISSP know the laws of their industry and region?
cards.answer: Because they must protect information while respecting these laws. The laws cover computer crimes, data leaks and privacy. They also cover licenses, rights over ideas, import and export rules, and data moving between countries.
cards.explanation: The rules depend on where you work and on what your company does.
cards.explanation_more: Source: (ISC)2 manual, domain 1, section “Understand legal and regulatory issues”. The manual lists: cybercrimes and data breaches. It also lists: licensing and intellectual property, import and export controls, transborder data flow and privacy. These topics come up in the next galaxies.

paragraphes: Julie spends a week at a school in another country. She takes out her phone in class, like at home.
The supervisor takes it away. At this school, phones are banned. The rules of her own school have no power here.
Knowing who has the right to set the rules in a given place is the question of jurisdiction.

decouverte.titre: Each place has its own head teacher
decouverte.comme: Each school has its head teacher. They decide at their school, not at the school next door. The football club has its coach, who decides for the club.
decouverte.enVrai: A jurisdiction is the official power to make decisions and judgments in a specific area. A company can fall under several jurisdictions at once. The picture stops there: a student has only one head teacher.

decouverte.question: An online shop based in one country sells to customers in another country. Who may have a say over its rules?
options: Maybe both countries, depending on the agreements between them
decouverte.answer: Maybe both countries, depending on the agreements between them
decouverte.explanation: Geography is not enough. Official agreements between countries (treaties) and what the company does also count.

decouverte.texte: A payment company has its head office, meaning its main office, in one country. Its servers are in a second country. Its customers live in ten other countries. Several authorities may say: “Here, you follow our rules.” This is why experts do not only look at the map.

cards.question: Official definition: “jurisdiction”
cards.answer: Jurisdiction is a legal concept that establishes the official power to make legal decisions and judgments.
cards.explanation: Think of your head teacher: they have the power to decide at their school.
cards.explanation_more: Definition from the official (ISC)2 manual, domain 1, section “Legislative and Regulatory Requirements”.

cards.question: Jurisdiction is a legal concept that establishes the [[official]] power to make legal decisions and [[judgments]].
cards.answer: Jurisdiction is a legal concept that establishes the official power to make legal decisions and judgments.
cards.explanation: The key words: an official power, and decisions and judgments.

cards.question: Jurisdiction is a [[legal concept]] that establishes the [[official power]] to make [[legal decisions]] and judgments.
cards.answer: Jurisdiction is a legal concept that establishes the official power to make legal decisions and judgments.
cards.explanation: Three blocks: a legal concept, an official power, and legal decisions.

cards.question: Write from memory the official definition of “jurisdiction”.
cards.answer: Jurisdiction is a legal concept that establishes the official power to make legal decisions and judgments.
cards.explanation: Remember the trio: power, official, decisions and judgments.

cards.question: A company sells to customers in several countries. To know which rules apply, what must it look at?
cards.answer: Geography, treaties and its type of activity
cards.explanation: The manual says it is not enough to know the geography or the political borders.
cards.explanation_more: Source: (ISC)2 manual, domain 1. Jurisdiction can also be influenced by international treaties and agreements, the activity of the organization, or other factors.
options: Geography, treaties and its type of activity
Only the country where its head office is
Only the language its customers speak
options_why: Geography matters, but the manual says it is not enough.
Language has no legal power. What counts are the authorities.

cards.question: Is knowing a company's country enough to know its jurisdiction?
cards.answer: No: treaties and activity count too
cards.explanation: The manual says geography alone is not enough.
options: No: treaties and activity count too

cards.question: Why must a security professional know the fine details of the jurisdictions they work in?
cards.answer: Because jurisdiction says who has the power to set the rules. Rules change from one place to another. Getting the jurisdiction wrong means applying the wrong rules.
cards.explanation: Same facts, other place: other rule.
cards.explanation_more: Source: (ISC)2 manual, domain 1: practitioners must know the nuances of the jurisdictions where they operate.

cards.question: What is the first difficulty in finding compliance requirements?
cards.answer: Knowing which jurisdiction has the legal power to set these requirements.
cards.explanation: Before reading the rules, you must know who has the right to write them.
cards.explanation_more: Source: (ISC)2 manual, domain 1, section “Legislative and Regulatory Requirements”.

cards.question: Besides geography, name two things that can influence jurisdiction.
cards.answer: International treaties and agreements, and the activity of the organization.
cards.explanation: The manual adds that other factors can also play a part.
cards.explanation_more: Source: (ISC)2 manual, domain 1: “international treaties and agreements, the activity of your organization, or any number of other factors”.

cards.question: Jurisdiction does not depend only on [[geography]]. It also depends on [[treaties]] between countries.
cards.answer: Jurisdiction does not depend only on geography. It also depends on treaties between countries.
cards.explanation: A map is not enough to know who decides.

cards.question: To know which jurisdiction applies, which box does each item go in?
cards.answer: Geography: the country of the offices and the border between two regions. Other factor: the agreement between two countries and what the company does.
cards.explanation: Geography is the place. The other factors are agreements and activity.

items.text: The country where the company has its offices
The border between two regions
An agreement signed between two countries
What the company does: sell, treat patients, host data

cards.question: What if a company ignores its jurisdiction?
cards.answer: It does not know who has the power to impose rules on it. It risks missing some duties or applying the wrong rules.
cards.explanation: This is the first difficulty of compliance.

cards.question: A start-up has customers in three countries. Explain to your boss why it must find out about the jurisdiction of each one.
cards.answer: Each country may have the power to set rules. You must look at geography, but also at treaties and at the start-up's activity.
cards.explanation: A map is not enough.

paragraphes: The teachers vote on a rule: no phones in class. This is the big principle.
Then the head teacher writes a more precise note: phones stay switched off at the bottom of your bag. This note explains how to apply the rule.
Both count. But if the note went against the voted rule, the voted rule would win. Law works the same way: it has two levels.

decouverte.comme: The principle voted by the teachers is the basic rule. The head teacher's note adds detail, but it stays below: it cannot go against it.
decouverte.enVrai: A law is a rule that has consequences if you break it. Either a criminal punishment, like a fine or prison. Or civil liability: having to repair the harm done to someone. Laws have two parts: statutes, written by parliament, and regulations, which are more detailed. The picture stops there: a school note does not send anyone to a judge.

decouverte.question: A text voted by parliament and a detailed text from an agency contradict each other. Which one wins?
options: The detailed text from the agency
decouverte.explanation: Both are mandatory. But the detailed text is subordinate to the voted text: it is there to apply it, not to go against it.

cards.answer: In U.S. law, the word law refers to any rule that, if broken, subjects a party to criminal punishment or civil liability.

cards.explanation_more: Definition from the official (ISC)2 manual, domain 1, section “Legislative and Regulatory Requirements”. Civil liability: the duty to repair the harm done to someone.

cards.question: Official definition: “statutes” and “regulations”
cards.answer: Laws may be generally categorized into two parts: statutes and regulations. Statutes are written and adopted by the jurisdiction's legislative body (e.g., U.S. Congress), while regulations are more detailed rules on how the execution of a statute will be performed.

paragraphes: Karim arrives late. He gets a one-hour detention.
Lina forges her school report. She goes before the discipline board.
The school ranks mistakes by how serious they are. The law does the same. In the United States, two words come up all the time: misdemeanor and felony.

decouverte.comme: A detention for a small slip. An expulsion for a serious fault. The heavier the fault, the heavier the punishment.
decouverte.enVrai: U.S. law ranks criminal offenses in the same way. A misdemeanor is a lighter offense. A felony is a more serious offense, with heavier penalties. The picture stops there: these are not school punishments, but categories of the justice system.

decouverte.question: In the United States, from how many months of possible prison do we talk about a felony?
decouverte.explanation: The manual sets the limit at 12 months. Below it, it is a misdemeanor. Above it, it is a felony.

decouverte.texte: The same kind of offense does not have the same name everywhere. In France, Germany and Switzerland, serious offenses are called crimes. Less serious ones are called misdemeanors or delicts (a delict is a less serious offense). In Brazil, people use the word contravention.

cards.answer: In U.S. law, a misdemeanor is any "lesser" criminal act that is punishable by less than 12 months in prison.

cards.answer: It is a felony: a more serious offense. It goes beyond 12 months of prison and carries heavier penalties.

decouverte.titre: One set of rules for every office
paragraphes: The government owns thousands of computers. They hold sensitive information: citizens' files, official documents.
If every office invents its own protection rules, some will be well protected and others will not.
So a law sets a minimum for everyone. In the United States, the first one is called the Computer Security Act (1987). In 2002, it was replaced by FISMA.

decouverte.comme: The education ministry sets a safety minimum for all schools: doors locked with a key, a visitors' register. A school can do better, never less.
decouverte.enVrai: The Computer Security Act asks for minimum security practices for the computers of the federal government. This is the central U.S. government. It also asks for policies so that each agency follows this minimum. FISMA, in 2002, takes the idea and extends it. The picture stops there: the 1987 text is aimed at the government, not at companies.

paragraphes: Your sports club sells shares to its fans. The treasurer says everything is fine.
In truth, he hides losses so that people keep buying. When the truth comes out, nobody trusts the club anymore.
In the United States, several big accounting scandals broke out in companies. In 2002, a law was passed to rebuild trust: the Sarbanes-Oxley Act (SOX).

decouverte.comme: For fans to keep trusting the club, it must be open. The treasurer cannot decide on spending that benefits himself: that is a conflict of interest. The accounts are checked. If he lies, he is punished. Anyone who finds cheating can report it safely.
decouverte.enVrai: SOX asks the same of publicly traded companies, meaning those where anyone can buy a small share. They must set up controls, give investors information about risks, and punish executives who lie. They must also protect whistleblowers. These are people who report wrongdoing to regulators, the authorities that watch over an industry. The picture stops there: SOX targets big companies, not your club.

decouverte.enVrai: PCI DSS is the rulebook of the bank card brands. It applies to everyone who takes, keeps or processes card payments. It is not a law: it is a standard required by contract. The picture stops there: PCI DSS applies almost everywhere in the world, not in just one mall.

cards.answer: Because more and more of our personal data goes online. Regulators, organizations and users worry about it.
